title: Biological analogy limitations
terms: A numerical weighted sum and activation.
A living cell with much richer dynamics.
explanation: The neuron analogy motivates connected units but does not make a network a literal brain. Our unit calculates z = wx + b. Real biological neurons involve temporal signals, chemistry and many mechanisms absent here. Name the numerical operation precisely instead of claiming human-like understanding from a diagram.
why: A precise model is easier to reason about than an exaggerated analogy.
question: Does this calculation reproduce a complete biological neuron?
choices: No; it is a simplified mathematical unit
Yes; the weighted sum models all biological mechanisms
reason: The chosen equation defines only a small computational model.
mistake: Treating biological vocabulary as proof of intelligence.
debug: Identify three biological mechanisms absent from this equation.
project: Explain a numerical neuron to someone without using the word brain.

title: Perceptron and XOR
terms: A weighted sum followed by a threshold.
A straight separating line in two dimensions.
One if exactly one binary input is one.
explanation: For XOR, targets for (0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1) are 0,1,1,0. A single linear threshold cannot separate the two positive corners from both negatives. Inspect all four predictions. Changing bias can improve one corner while worsening another; hidden nonlinear units can solve the problem.
why: This limitation motivates multilayer networks.
question: Can any single linear threshold classify all four XOR corners?
choices: Yes; simply increase the bias enough
No; they are not linearly separable
reason: The positive and negative corners are interleaved; one straight boundary cannot separate them.
mistake: Checking only two of the four truth-table rows.
debug: The OR preset gets three XOR cases right, but still fails (1,1).
project: Construct AND and OR gates, then combine hidden gates to represent XOR.

title: Weights and biases
terms: An additive offset independent of the input.
explanation: Multiply each input by its corresponding weight, sum, then add the bias once. A negative weight reverses the sign of its contribution. Bias can shift a decision boundary even when inputs are zero. Changing a weight has no effect when its input is zero.
why: Weights express sensitivity to inputs; bias sets a baseline.
question: What contributes when all inputs equal zero?
choices: The bias
The sum of the weights alone
reason: Each weighted input becomes zero, leaving only the offset.
mistake: Multiplying the bias by an input.
debug: Set both inputs to zero in the sandbox and inspect the contributions.
project: Choose weights for z = 2x₁ - x₂ + 3 and test a negative input.

title: Linear layers
terms: A linear transformation plus a bias.
One dot product with a column of weights, plus its bias.
explanation: A dense layer applies the same affine operation to every example. Multiple output units use different weight columns. Our panel computes one output from two inputs; the forward lab extends this to more layers. Two affine layers without a nonlinear activation combine into one affine transformation.
why: The layer equation is the foundation of neural computation.
question: Why insert nonlinear activations between dense layers?
choices: To make matrix dimensions disappear
To represent functions beyond one affine transformation
reason: Composing affine transformations remains affine; nonlinearities expand expressive power.
mistake: Calling every affine output a probability.
debug: A raw affine output can be negative or exceed one.
project: Compose two affine layers on paper and simplify them into one.

title: Sigmoid, tanh, ReLU and leaky ReLU
terms: A function applied to a preactivation.
A region with very small local sensitivity.
explanation: Sigmoid maps to (0,1); tanh maps to (-1,1). ReLU keeps positive inputs and maps negatives to zero. Leaky ReLU retains a scaled negative branch. The panel displays all four results and asks for leaky ReLU. Sigmoid and tanh saturate at large magnitudes. ReLU has a corner at zero, where a chosen subgradient convention is needed.
why: Nonlinear activations let stacked layers represent more than affine functions.
formula: leaky ReLU(z) = z if z ≥ 0, otherwise αz
question: What does ordinary ReLU return for a negative input?
choices: Zero
The unchanged negative input
reason: Ordinary ReLU clips negatives; leaky ReLU keeps a scaled negative value.
mistake: Using the derivative of sigmoid when the layer uses ReLU.
debug: At z = -2, ordinary ReLU is 0 but leaky ReLU with α = 0.1 is -0.2.
project: Compare outputs and local derivatives at -2, 0 and 2.

title: Stable softmax
terms: A raw score before probability normalization.
Exponentials normalized to sum to one.
Subtract a shared maximum before exponentiation.
explanation: Exponentiating logits like 1000 directly can overflow. Subtracting their maximum preserves softmax probabilities because the common scale cancels. For logits [1000,1001], use [-1,0]. The first probability is exp(-1)/(exp(-1)+1). Each probability depends on all logits, unlike separate scalar sigmoid outputs.
why: Stable normalization prevents avoidable numerical failures.
question: Why can the maximum be subtracted from every logit?
choices: It changes the target class labels
The common exponential scale cancels in normalization
reason: Both numerator and denominator share the same factor; their ratio is unchanged.
mistake: Exponentiating very large raw logits directly.
debug: Compare [1000,1001] with [0,1]; the probabilities match.
project: Normalize three logits [2,1,0] and verify the probabilities sum to one.

title: Initialization
terms: Units behaving identically because their parameters match.
A variance-based choice commonly used with ReLU.
explanation: Identical zero weights in a hidden layer can make units receive identical updates, preventing useful specialization. Random initialization breaks symmetry. He normal initialization uses variance 2/fan-in, hence standard deviation sqrt(2/fan-in), under its assumptions. The panel calculates the scale, not a random sample. One initializer is not suitable for every activation.
why: Appropriate scale helps prevent unstable signals and gradients.
question: Why avoid identical hidden-unit weights?
choices: They can stay symmetric under identical updates
Every zero weight makes the software crash
reason: The mathematical symmetry prevents units from learning distinct features.
mistake: Confusing variance with standard deviation.
debug: For fan-in 8, variance is 0.25 and standard deviation is 0.5.
project: Compare He and Xavier scale assumptions for ReLU and tanh.

title: Shape, rank and dtype
terms: Number of axes, not matrix algebra rank here.
explanation: Shape (2,3) means two rows of three values. Tensor rank is two because there are two axes; there are six elements. float32 uses four payload bytes per element, giving 24 bytes. A vector of length 100 has tensor rank one. Scalar shape () has rank zero.
why: Correct shape and dtype reasoning prevents errors before a layer runs.
formula: payload = rows × columns × bytes per element
question: What is the tensor rank of shape (4,3)?
choices: Twelve
Two
reason: Rank counts axes; twelve is the element count.
mistake: Confusing element count, tensor rank and matrix linear-algebra rank.
debug: A 2×3 matrix can have matrix rank at most two, but its tensor rank is always two.
project: Run the Python NumPy inspector and verify shape, dtype and payload.

title: Broadcasting
terms: Align trailing dimensions and expand axes of length one.
Equal lengths, or at least one length equal to one.
explanation: A matrix of shape (2,2) can add a column of shape (2,1). Each row offset repeats across that row. For matrix rows [1,2] and [1,2], offsets [10,20] yield [11,12] and [21,22]. Shapes (2,2) and (3,) are incompatible because trailing lengths two and three cannot match.
why: Broadcasting expresses useful repeated operations while shape mistakes can silently change meaning.
question: Can trailing axis lengths two and three broadcast?
choices: No; neither is one and they differ
Yes; any two shapes can add
reason: Compatible trailing axes must match or have length one.
mistake: Adding a row vector when a column offset was intended.
debug: Compare (2,1) offsets with (1,2) offsets and explain the different repetition.
project: Write the output of a 2×3 matrix plus a 1×3 row.

title: Indexing and slicing
terms: An axis position, starting at zero.
A selected range with an exclusive stop.
explanation: For [10,20,30,40], slice [1:3] selects 20 and 30. It includes index one and excludes index three. Indexing may remove an axis; slicing usually retains it. Negative indices count from the end in Python, though this teaching control uses nonnegative bounds.
why: Precise selection is necessary for batches, features and image crops.
question: Is the stop index included in a Python slice?
choices: Yes; it is always included
No; the stop is exclusive
reason: An exclusive stop makes adjacent slices line up without overlapping endpoints.
mistake: Expecting [1:3] to contain three items.
debug: Its length is stop - start = 2 for this unit-step slice.
project: Split [10,20,30,40] into two non-overlapping slices and reconstruct it.

title: Memory layout and views
terms: A different interpretation of shared array memory.
Another reference to the same underlying object or memory.
explanation: A view can share data, so modifying it can modify the original array. A copy separates storage. Our panel uses a Python list alias to illustrate shared mutation of [1,2,3]; it does not claim to implement NumPy strides. In NumPy, basic slicing usually returns views while advanced indexing returns copies. Shape changes alone do not guarantee a copy.
why: Unexpected shared mutation can corrupt inputs or cached intermediate values.
formula: write through alias; then sum original
target: sum of the original after mutation
question: Does modifying a copy necessarily modify the original?
choices: No; copies have separate element storage
Yes; all selections share storage
reason: The distinction depends on memory sharing, not merely variable names.
mistake: Assuming every selected array owns independent storage.
debug: Predict the original after changing a basic NumPy slice, then compare with slice.copy().
project: Draw shared buffers for a view and independent buffers for a copy.

title: float16, float32 and float64
terms: How finely a format distinguishes representable values.
explanation: Finite precision means some nearby integers or decimals become the same stored value. This panel runs NumPy conversions to float16, float32 or float64 in Python, using ties to even. float16 has fewer fraction bits and a smaller range; float32 balances memory and precision; float64 is useful for sensitive numerical checks. More bits increase payload but do not fix every algorithmic error.
why: Rounding affects small updates, loss stability and gradient checks.
formula: represented value = rounding to the selected binary format
question: Can distinct input values become equal after low-precision rounding?
choices: No; every real number is represented exactly
Yes; the format has a finite set of values
reason: A finite bit pattern cannot represent infinitely many real numbers.
mistake: Using low precision for a sensitive finite-difference check.
debug: Compare 4096 and 4097 in float16; explain why one unit can disappear.
project: Compare 16777217 in float32 and float64 and calculate the rounding error.

title: Device placement
terms: The processor/memory location used by a tensor.
explanation: CPU and GPU tensors generally cannot participate in the same operation without a compatible transfer. Move both model and data to the intended device. A transfer can dominate a tiny computation, so GPU is not automatically faster. Our device labels illustrate compatibility; they do not allocate real GPU tensors.
why: Device mismatches cause runtime failures even when dimensions are correct.
formula: compatible = one if both operands are on the same device
question: What should be checked besides tensor shapes?
choices: Device and dtype compatibility
Only the variable names
reason: Shape equality does not move memory or reconcile devices.
mistake: Moving input data but leaving model parameters on CPU.
debug: Describe the transfer needed when data is GPU and weights are CPU.
project: Draw CPU storage, a transfer boundary and GPU computation; identify what moves.

title: Autograd graphs
terms: An operation or value in a computation.
A route from a parameter to the loss.
explanation: For y = s × x × x, x appears on two multiplication inputs. Each route contributes to the derivative, so dy/dx = sx + sx = 2sx. Automatic differentiation records operations and applies their local derivative rules. It is not the same as perturbing parameters or generating a symbolic formula for every possible program.
why: Shared parameters require adding contributions from every use.
question: What happens when a parameter affects loss along two routes?
choices: Keep only the last route
Add the gradient contributions from both routes
reason: The total sensitivity is the sum of path contributions.
mistake: Forgetting one occurrence of a reused variable.
debug: Treating x×x as if only one operand depended on x gives half the correct derivative.
project: Draw the graph for y = 3x² + x and calculate its derivative.

title: Dense layer shapes
explanation: Using the row-vector convention, X has shape (B,D), W has shape (D,H), and Y = XW + b has shape (B,H). A bias of shape (H,) broadcasts across B examples. The shared inner D dimensions contract. The panel counts output elements; zero cells are shape placeholders, not computed predictions.
why: Writing shapes first catches incompatible layers early.
question: Which dimensions must match for XW?
choices: The input width D of X and first axis of W
Batch size B and output width H
reason: The inner dimensions contract in matrix multiplication.
mistake: Using a transposed weight convention without updating the equation.
debug: Some libraries store W as (H,D); their forward operation uses its transpose.
project: Track shapes through widths 3 -> 4 -> 2 for a batch of five.

title: Batch axis
terms: The axis distinguishing values within an example.
explanation: Increasing batch size adds examples, not features or new model parameters. A batch of three rows with four features can feed the same weights as a batch of one row with four features. The output preserves the batch axis. Aggregate losses deliberately over examples; do not accidentally mix batch and feature reductions.
why: Batch semantics determine how predictions and gradients are averaged.
question: Does a larger batch automatically add model weights?
choices: Yes; every example needs separate weights
No; examples share the same layer parameters
reason: A layer reuses its weight matrix for every row.
mistake: Interpreting the first axis as features after batching.
debug: Write shapes for an unbatched vector (4,) and batched inputs (3,4).
project: Calculate parameter count for a 4-to-2 dense layer: 8 weights and 2 biases.

title: Matrix multiplication
terms: A dot product defining one matrix output.
explanation: For A = [[1,2],[3,4]] and B = [[1,2],[3,4]], A@B is [[7,10],[15,22]]. The bottom-right result is 3×2 + 4×4 = 22. Elementwise multiplication would produce [[1,4],[9,16]], a different operation. The panel uses editable A and fixed B.
why: Dense layers compute many weighted sums with matrix multiplication.
question: Is matrix multiplication the same as multiplying matching entries?
choices: No; each output combines a row and a column
Yes; both operations are identical
reason: The sum over the inner axis distinguishes matrix multiplication.
mistake: Multiplying row i by row j rather than column j.
debug: For bottom-right output, select A row one and B column one with zero-based indexing.
project: Compute a 2×3 by 3×1 multiplication and annotate each term.

title: Layer composition
terms: An intermediate representation between input and output.
Feeding one operation result into the next.
explanation: This small network computes hidden = ReLU(w₁x + b₁), then output = w₂hidden + b₂. With x = 2, w₁ = 3, b₁ = -1, hidden = 5. With w₂ = 2 and b₂ = 1, output = 11. An inactive hidden ReLU makes its input-dependent contribution zero.
why: Following intermediate values explains the final prediction.
question: When hidden ReLU is zero, what remains at this output?
choices: The original input x unchanged
The output bias b₂
reason: The weighted hidden term is zero, leaving the output offset.
mistake: Applying the activation to the wrong layer or skipping it.
debug: Compare the same network with hidden ReLU versus a linear hidden activation.
project: Trace two hidden units and one output in the forward propagation lab.

title: Logits versus probabilities
terms: A normalized value interpreted under a model.
explanation: Raw logits can be negative, positive or much larger than one. Softmax converts a set of logits to nonnegative numbers summing to one. Larger logits increase relative probability, but probabilities still require calibration for reliable confidence claims. A predicted class usually selects the largest score or probability.
why: Correct interpretation prevents treating raw scores as confidence percentages.
question: Can a raw logit of 3 mean probability 300%?
choices: No; a logit is not a probability
Yes; multiplying by 100 always produces valid confidence
reason: Normalize with the model-appropriate function; probabilities cannot exceed one.
mistake: Applying softmax twice to already normalized probabilities.
debug: Compare argmax of [1,0] with argmax of its softmax.
project: Compute softmax and distinguish class choice from calibrated confidence.

title: Training versus inference
terms: Behavior used for prediction after training.
Values deciding which activations are retained.
explanation: Training can use randomness such as dropout and batch statistics. Inference generally disables dropout and uses learned normalization statistics. In inverted dropout, a kept activation is divided by its keep probability during training; inference returns the activation unchanged. A fixed mask is shown here for reproducibility, not sampled randomly.
why: Forgetting the mode can produce inconsistent predictions.
formula: training output = x × mask/(1 - drop probability)
question: What does inverted dropout do during inference?
choices: It uses a fresh random mask every time
It returns the activation without dropping or rescaling it
reason: Training scaling already preserves the expected activation.
mistake: Leaving the network in training mode during evaluation.
debug: For x = 2 and drop rate 0.5, kept output is 4 or dropped output is 0; expectation is 2.
project: Explain why inference output is 2 for both displayed training masks.
